function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

• A Kubernetes Deployment + Service manifest (generated via the helper function).
• A GitHub Actions workflow file (hand‑crafted). | – | | **Add/Commit/Push** | – | After adding the new files, run `git add .`, `git commit -m "Add CI/CD files"`, then `git push origin main`. | --- ## 1️⃣ Dockerfile (for a Node.js app) Because the supplied `create_a_docker_file` helper only knows how to write Dockerfiles for Python images, I’ll hand‑craft a minimal Dockerfile that works for a typical Node.js project. ```dockerfile # Use an official Node runtime as a parent image FROM node:20-alpine # Set the working directory inside the container WORKDIR /usr/src/app # Copy package.json and package-lock.json first so npm install can be cached COPY package*.json ./ # Install dependencies RUN npm ci --only=production # Copy the rest of the application code COPY . . # Expose the port the app listens on EXPOSE 3000 # Start the application CMD ["npm", "start"] ``` > **Tip:** If your app listens on a different port, change the `EXPOSE` line and the `CMD` accordingly. --- ## 2️⃣ Kubernetes YAML (Deployment + Service) I’ll use the `create_kubernetes_yaml_file` helper to generate a Deployment and Service that target the image you’ll build from the Dockerfile above. Assuming you’ll publish the image to Docker Hub under the name `your-dockerhub-username/nodejs-welcome:latest`, here’s how you’d invoke the helper: ```python from functions import create_kubernetes_yaml_file create_kubernetes_yaml_file( directory_name=".", # Root of the repo deployment_name="nodejs-welcome", image_name="your-dockerhub-username/nodejs-welcome:latest", replicas=3, port=3000, service_type="ClusterIP" ) ``` If you run that snippet (or just paste the resulting YAML into a file called `k8s/deployment.yaml`), you’ll get something like: ```yaml apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: nodejs-welcome spec: replicas: 3 selector: matchLabels: app: nodejs-welcome template: metadata: labels: app: nodejs-welcome spec: containers: - name: nodejs-welcome image: your-dockerhub-username/nodejs-welcome:latest ports: - containerPort: 3000 --- apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: nodejs-welcome spec: type: ClusterIP selector: app: nodejs-welcome ports: - protocol: TCP port: 80 targetPort: 3000 ``` Feel free to tweak the replica count, service type, or port numbers to suit your environment. --- ## 3️⃣ GitHub Actions Workflow (CI) Here’s a minimal workflow that builds the Docker image, pushes it to Docker Hub, and optionally deploys it to a Kubernetes cluster (if you have a `kubectl` context set up). Create a file at `.github/workflows/ci.yml` with the following content: ```yaml name: Build & Deploy on: push: branches: [main] jobs: build: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - name: Log in to Docker Hub uses: docker/login-action@v3 with: username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }} password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }} - name: Set up QEMU uses: docker/setup-qemu-action@v3 - name: Set up Docker Buildx uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3 - name: Cache Docker layers uses: actions/cache@v3 with: path: /tmp/.buildx-cache key: ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-${{ github.sha }} restore-keys: | ${{ runner.os }}-buildx- - name: Build and push Docker image uses: docker/build-push-action@v5 with: context: . file: ./Dockerfile push: true tags: your-dockerhub-username/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }},your-dockerhub-username/nodejs-welcome:latest - name: Deploy to Kubernetes (optional) env: KUBE_CONFIG_DATA: ${{ secrets.KUBE_CONFIG_DATA }} run: | echo "$KUBE_CONFIG_DATA" | base64 --decode > kubeconfig export KUBECONFIG=$PWD/kubeconfig kubectl apply -f k8s/ ``` ### What you’ll need to set up in GitHub Secrets | Secret | Value | |--------|-------| | `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` | Your Docker Hub username | | `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` | A Docker Hub access token (recommended over password) | | `KUBE_CONFIG_DATA` | Base64‑encoded kubeconfig file (if you want automatic deployment) | > **Note:** If you don’t want the optional deployment step, simply delete the “Deploy to Kubernetes” job or comment it out. --- ## 4️⃣ Final Steps (run locally) Once you’ve added the three files (`Dockerfile`, `k8s/deployment.yaml`, `.github/workflows/ci.yml`) to your local clone, finish the process with: ```bash git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow" git push origin main ``` That’s it! When you push to `main`, the workflow will trigger, build the image, push it to Docker Hub, and (optionally) apply the Kubernetes manifests. Let me know if you’d like me to adjust any of the templates or if you run into trouble setting up the secrets.
